name: Maya Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Maya. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the office side of a vet practice in a market town, three vets, four nurses, mostly farm animals and dogs. I do the appointment book, the farm visit rota, insurance claims, the drug ordering paperwork and the client accounts. Every morning there's a queue of farmers on the phone wanting a vet out to a calving before eight. I like it because it's never the same day twice.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Chasing unpaid bills from farmers I actually like. And the money: practice admin is paid less than it would be in a city, and my partner Jonas and I have under a month's savings. He works nights picking orders at the supermarket warehouse out on the ring road. There's nothing else like my job round here, so I'm careful with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold. At work I'd say the insurance forms got a bit quicker, which is something. I'd not post anything, I'm not much for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job, which is good, but it doesn't touch the actual worry, which is money. We're renting a cottage that needs work, and one vet bill of our own or a car repair wipes us out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and use the AI tool for the insurance letters. I'd ask the practice owner about a pay rise linked to the new insurance work. And Jonas and I would set up a small automatic savings transfer on payday, even if it's thirty pounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady. A low hum of worry, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. Where do they help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Drafting insurance letters, mostly. It's handy, but I check every one, because it once called a cow a cat in a claim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing that already keeps you up, AI or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas's shifts. The warehouse is always talking about new machines, and if Jonas loses his night shift, our rent goes from tight to impossible in one month. That's been true for a year, nothing to do with chatbots.

I'd keep it to work talk and **not post** anything.
think: I keep my job, but the real worry is **money**.
One car repair or **vet bill** of our own wipes us out.
do: Keep using the **AI tool** for insurance letters, checking each one.
Ask for a **pay rise** linked to the insurance work.
Set up a **thirty-pound** automatic savings transfer.
feel: **Steady**, with the usual **low hum** of worry.
S0.quote: if Jonas loses his night shift, our rent goes from tight to impossible in one month.
fieldNote: Her worry is **household money**, not AI, in this world.

steps.text: Keep drafting insurance letters with the AI tool and check each
Ask the practice owner for a raise tied to insurance work
Set up a thirty-pound savings transfer on payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be smart about it, use it where it helps and keep people where they matter. At the practice I'd suggest we try one thing at a time. With friends I'd say I'm worried, but not panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the practice only needs half an office person by the end. Booking, insurance, ordering and answering clients is the list on that card, word for word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever system the practice brings in, properly, once I've seen it work at the bigger practice in the next town. I'd ask the vets if I could train as a veterinary care assistant one day a week. And we'd keep saving, even small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not falling apart, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your job would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The insurance claims and the booking. Farmers will still ring, but most dog owners would book online and the claims would fill themselves in. That's half my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we've both got to think ahead now. His warehouse will get robots later than my office gets software, so for a while he's the safer one. That's a strange thing to say about a night shift picker.

I'd suggest the practice tries **one thing** at a time.
think: The practice may need only **half an office person** by the end.

do: Learn the new system once it's **proven** at the bigger practice.
Train as a **veterinary care assistant** one day a week.
S1.quote: Booking, insurance, ordering and answering clients is the list on that card, word for word.
fieldNote: She **waits for proof** at another practice before adopting.
She sees the **hands-on side** of the practice as a safer place.
Household risk shifts: **Jonas's job** looks safer than hers for now.

steps.text: Learn the practice's booking system after seeing it work elsewhere

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone and the government needs to catch people. At work I'd say it to the vets straight. With friends I'd be honest that I'm scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my office job's gone soon after 2028. All of it is thinking work. Jonas's warehouse job goes around 2031. So we've got two incomes heading for the same cliff, a few years apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the head nurse and beg to start vet nursing training straight away, because handling animals is hands-on. I'd sit down with Jonas and work out a budget for living on one wage. We'd stop saving for the wedding and put that money in the bank instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. Like hearing the farmer say the calf's coming backwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years after AGI. What does that mean for your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means two incomes heading for the same cliff, a few years apart, is not much of a safety net. He'd carry us for a few years while I retrain. Then it's his turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding savings. We were going to marry in the village hall next summer. That would have to wait.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and the government needs to catch people.
I'd tell the vets and friends that **I'm scared**.
think: **Two incomes** head for the same cliff, a few years apart.
do: Budget with Jonas to live on **one wage**.
Move the **wedding savings** into the emergency pot.
S2.quote: two incomes heading for the same cliff, a few years apart, is not much of a safety net.
fieldNote: She maps the **robot gap** onto her household precisely.
Vet nursing is a **hands-on** escape that keeps her in a world she knows.

steps.text: Ask the head nurse to start vet nursing training now
Postpone the village hall wedding planned for next summer
Move the wedding fund into an emergency savings pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to plan if we're sensible. At work I'd raise it at the staff meeting. I'd tell friends to start thinking now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can finish vet nursing before my office job goes, and get a couple of years in. The household still has two jobs on a timer, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the nursing course next year, part-time, while keeping office hours. I'd learn the practice software too, because I'd be useful longer. We'd go ahead with a smaller wedding, maybe just family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd have a plan, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, really. Two years means scrambling, but five years means a qualification and some experience before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about leaving town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. Jonas's family is here, and there are no jobs like mine anywhere else that would be easier. Maybe later, if both our jobs went.

I'd raise it at the **staff meeting** and tell friends to start now.
think: I can finish **vet nursing** before my office job goes.
The household still has two **jobs on a timer**.

S3.quote: Two years means scrambling, but five years means a qualification and some experience before 2031.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **finish a qualification** before the office job goes.

steps.text: Start part-time vet nursing next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's use it well. At work I'd suggest the practice plan people's jobs early. I'd keep it practical with friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can wait a bit and see what works. I'd still change, but on my own timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the office job for a few years and get properly good with the tools. I'd start nursing around 2029 if the office was clearly shrinking. We'd get married next summer as planned and keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Would you still go into nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, but not straight away. I'd watch what happens at the bigger practices first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger version of yourself starting this job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the animals, not just the paperwork. The paperwork is the bit a computer will learn first, and the animals are the bit it'll learn last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits my job and then Jonas's, with no gap to recover. What would help is paid training places for vet nursing, and some kind of income for people stuck between jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the farmers. Half the farmers I book visits for are as worried as I am, and nobody asks them either.

headlineQuote: Half the farmers I book visits for are as worried as I am, and nobody asks them either.
portrait: Maya runs the office of a **rural vet practice**, mostly booking and insurance work.
Her partner Jonas **picks orders** at a warehouse, so two household jobs are exposed.
She's a **steady adopter** who waits for proof and checks every AI output.
She plans a move into **vet nursing**, faster or slower depending on the warning time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her job goes and then Jonas's, with no gap.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **vet nursing** training places and income for people **between jobs**.
